abstract.p: Therapy-related myeloid neoplasm (tMN) is a fatal consequence of exposure to cytotoxic therapy administered in the treatment of cancer. Individuals with pre-existing TP53 clonal hematopoiesis (CH) are at high risk of tMN, with avoidance of therapy being the only strategy to reduce tMN risk. Here, in four randomized clinical trials, we show that the CDK4/6 inhibitor trilaciclib, given in conjunction with a variety of chemotherapeutic regimens and across diverse populations of patients with cancer, mitigates chemotherapy-related expansion of CH clones with mutations in DNA damage response genes, including TP53. This finding was also observed in a syngeneic mouse model of TP53-mutant CH, demonstrating that CDK4/6 inhibition blocks platinum-induced TP53 competitive repopulation through promoting hematopoietic stem and progenitor quiescence and decreasing the stemness advantage of TP53-mutant clones. This represents a proof of concept for a potential pharmacologic strategy to block chemotherapy-induced expansion of preleukemic TP53-mutant clones.

Analysis of clinical trial data suggests that CDK4/6 inhibitors prevent the expansion of TP53-mutant clones in the blood, potentially mitigating the risk of secondary myeloid neoplasms in patients treated with cytotoxic drugs.

sec.title: Main
sec.p: Myeloid neoplasms (MNs), including acute myeloid leukemia and high-risk myelodysplastic syndrome, have a median survival of less than 5 years and are highly resistant to therapy1,2. Established risk factors for MN include advancing age and prior exposure to oncologic therapy. Therapy-related MNs (tMNs) account for 15% MN cases and are almost universally fatal3,4. Clonal hematopoiesis (CH), whereby a hematopoietic stem or progenitor cell (HSPC) acquires a mutation that confers a selective advantage, is common with aging5,6. However, in a small subset of individuals, CH clones will expand and acquire additional mutations, eventually leading to hematologic cancers, particularly MN7,8.

Mutations in DNA damage response (DDR) pathway members, including TP53, CHEK2 and PPM1D, confer an advantage through suppression of apoptosis in response to DNA damage9–11. Thus, DDR CH clones show a fitness advantage in the setting of environmental stressors such as cytotoxic therapy12,13. We and others have previously shown that expansion of TP53-mutant CH under the selective pressure of cytotoxic therapy is the major driver of tMN10,12,14. Despite advances in the ability to identify solid tumor patients with CH at high risk of tMN based on genomic and clinical features12, there are no therapeutic strategies that prevent tMN. Due to the difficulty in treating tMN, early intervention by prevention of CH expansion may be the highest-yield strategy to eradicate this lethal disease.

Cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) are critical regulators of cell-cycle progression, with CDK4 and CDK6 driving progression through the G1/S checkpoint by phosphorylating the tumor suppressor retinoblastoma protein (RB)15. CDK4/6 is hyperactivated to promote uncontrolled proliferation in select tumors with intact RB, including hormone-responsive breast cancers, which has led to the development of CDK4/6 inhibitors as antitumor agents15. Bone marrow (BM) HSPCs are highly dependent upon CDK4/6 for cell-cycle regulation16. As such, pharmacologic quiescence of HSPCs by CDK4/6 inhibition has been shown to prevent cytopenias and prolong survival in mice exposed to chemotherapy or lethal doses of radiation16,17.While many tumors are CDK4/6-dependent, roughly 10% adult and pediatric cancers are functionally CDK4/6-independent due to RB inactivation18. Cancer types with frequent RB inactivation include most small-cell lung cancers (SCLCs)19, triple-negative breast cancer20, bladder cancer21, human papillomavirus-associated head and neck cancer22, osteosarcoma23 and metastatic prostate cancer24, where cytotoxic therapy is the standard of care. The transient arrest of HSPCs through CDK4/6 inhibition before chemotherapy administration in patients with RB-inactivated tumors has the potential to protect HSPCs from chemotherapy-induced genotoxic stress, without adversely impacting the antitumor effects of chemotherapy18.

Trilaciclib is an intravenously administered, small-molecule CDK4/6 inhibitor that is Food and Drug Administration-approved as an adjunctive preventive therapy in patients with extensive-stage SCLC (ES-SCLC) receiving a platinum/etoposide-containing or topotecan-containing regimen to decrease the incidence of chemotherapy-induced myelosuppression25. We hypothesized that, by protecting HSPCs from the cytotoxic effects of chemotherapy, trilaciclib and other CDK4/6 inhibitors reduce the fitness advantage of TP53-mutant CH, thus decreasing its competitive repopulation within the HSPC pool. Given that chemotherapy-related expansion of TP53-mutant clones is a key step in the natural history of CH progression to tMN, we present data here for a proof-of-concept approach to mitigate CH expansion during cytotoxic therapy that could potentially reduce the incidence of tMN.

sec.title: Trilaciclib reduces DDR CH expansion during chemotherapy
sec.p:
We obtained serial blood samples from 65 individuals with ES-SCLC, pooled from two studies, undergoing first-line therapy with carboplatin and etoposide with or without atezolizumab who were randomized to receive trilaciclib (n = 28) or placebo (n = 37) on days 1, 2 and 3 before chemotherapy25 (Fig. 1a). This included a sample at baseline and after four 21-day cycles of trilaciclib or placebo. For each sample, we performed deep targeted error-corrected sequencing of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (MNCs) using a nine-gene CH panel, which enabled reliable detection of mutations down to 0.1% variant allele fraction (VAF26; Supplementary Table 1). As a comparator group, we obtained sequential blood samples from healthy individuals (n = 176) of similar age (Supplementary Table 2). Demographic features, including age, were similar between placebo and trilaciclib arms (Supplementary Table 2). Before therapy, individuals with ES-SCLC and cancer-free controls had a similar frequency of CH overall (71% and 72%, respectively), with CH prevalence increasing with age (Fig. 1b). DNMT3A and TET2 were the two most commonly mutated genes across both groups (Fig. 1c), and the majority (85%) of mutations occurred with a VAF of <1% across most genes (Fig. 1d).Fig. 1CDK4/6 inhibition with trilaciclib reduces the expansion of DDR CH during carboplatin/etoposide therapy.

The SCLC clinical trial image in a created in BioRender; Chan, I. https://BioRender.com/nadlvhb (2026). b, Frequency of detectable CH before receiving treatment within the patients with SCLC (blue) and healthy controls cohort (red) as a function of age with the shaded area representing the 95% confidence intervals. c, Pretreatment CH mutational landscape and gene distribution in patients with SCLC and healthy controls. d, VAF distribution of CH mutations before treatment. e, Proportion of individuals with CH after treatment among patients with SCLC and untreated individuals. Treated cohort is then further subdivided into placebo or trilaciclib arms with CH grouped as follows: DTA (DNMT3A, TET2, ASXL1) or DDR genes (TP53, PPM1D and CHEK2). f, Box plots of individual growth rates of DTA CH versus DDR CH mutations in the trilaciclib (green) and placebo arm (orange) compared to untreated healthy individuals (red) with the bar indicating the median, interquartile range shown as the box edges and whiskers extending to 1.5× the interquartile range. Each point represents individual CH growth rates used to derive the box plot. Differences in the proportion of individuals with CH were tested using logistic regression and differences in the growth rate of CH were tested using linear regression adjusted for age. As expected, after chemotherapy, we observed an increased frequency (45% ES-SCLC individuals) of CH in genes related to the DDR pathway, including TP53, PPM1D and CHEK2 (Fig. 1e), compared to only 22% untreated control individuals (P = 0.029). Notably, this increase was not driven by the acquisition of new mutations as 96% of all detectable CH mutations after therapy were present before therapy but at levels below the limit of detection (0.1%) for our assay (Supplementary Table 3). This supports previous observations that the association between chemotherapy and DDR CH is largely driven by expansion of pre-existing clones12. We then compared the frequency of CH after chemotherapy among ES-SCLC patients randomized to trilaciclib versus placebo. In the trilaciclib group, the frequency of DDR CH mutations decreased after therapy (29%) compared to the placebo arm (57%) whereas a similar frequency of DNMT3A, TET2 and ASXL1 (DTA) CH mutations was observed (Fig. 1e). To study change in CH dynamics over time, for each CH mutation, we calculated the exponential growth rate27,28, a metric supported by simulations of clonal evolutionary dynamics29. We hypothesized that the reduced frequency of DDR CH in the trilaciclib group might be explained by a lower DDR growth rate than in the placebo group. While DDR CH clones expanded more rapidly during chemotherapy in both the trilaciclib (P = 3.9 × 10−8) and placebo groups (P = 5.8 × 10−19) compared to untreated control individuals, the growth rate was significantly lower with trilaciclib compared to placebo (P = 0.039; Fig. 1f). Overall, the treatment with trilaciclib reduced the growth rate of chemotherapy-related DDR CH by 36% compared to placebo.

To determine whether the protective effect of trilaciclib on therapy-related CH expansion observed in patients treated with carboplatin and etoposide could be seen with other chemotherapeutic regimens, we obtained serial blood samples from two additional randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trials of trilaciclib—first, leucovorin/5-fluorouracil/oxaliplatin/irinotecan as well as bevacizumab among individuals (n = 125) with metastatic colorectal carcinoma (mCRC30 ; Fig. 2a); second, gemcitabine as well as carboplatin among women (n = 34) with metastatic triple-negative breast cancer (mTNBC31 ; Fig. 2b). We profiled CH at treatment onset and after 12 14-day cycles of chemotherapy for the mCRC trial and after 7 21-day cycles in the mTNBC trial. Similar to patients with ES-SCLC, we observed comparable frequencies of CH overall and DDR CH before therapy among patients with mCRC (20%), mTNBC (16%) and healthy controls (21%). Here again, a lower growth rate of therapy-induced DDR CH was observed in the trilaciclib arm compared to placebo in both the mCRC (P = 1.9 × 10−4, 26% decreased) and mTNBC (P = 0.014, 27% decreased) trials (Fig. 2c,d).Fig. 2CDK4/6 inhibition with trilaciclib reduces DDR CH expansion across multiple chemotherapeutic regimens.

To characterize whether the impact of trilaciclib on mitigating DDR CH expansion differs by gene, we pooled data from all clinical trials. We observed consistent effects across all three DDR CH genes included in our panel, with trilaciclib significantly reducing TP53 (P = 9.6 × 10−3) and PPM1D (P = 1.3 × 10−6) expansion during therapy (Fig. 2e). The spectrum of DDR CH mutations was similar between placebo and trilaciclib arms (Extended Data Fig. 1a–c).

We compared our results measuring change in CH dynamics as the percent change in VAF per month and observed a similar protective effect of trilaciclib (Supplementary Fig. 1)—average change in VAF per month of 0.06% for placebo and 0.03% for trilaciclib. Sensitivity analyses restricting variants with a VAF of ≥0.2% in at least one time point to explore the impact of very low VAF variants on our findings revealed consistent results regarding directionality and magnitude of the impact of trilaciclib on reducing the growth rate of DDR CH (Supplementary Fig. 2a–d).

Within all three genes, we observed heterogeneity in the growth rate of mutations with most clones expanding during therapy while some remained stable or even slightly decreased in VAF (Fig. 2e). We used multivariable regression to test for possible sources of heterogeneity in the growth rates of mutations within the same gene and gene class (DDR versus DTA) including treatment regimen, patient demographics (age, sex, race), change in blood counts during treatment and hotspot status for missense variants (as measured by the number of reported mutations within COSMIC32; Extended Data Fig. 1d–f and Supplementary Tables 4 and 5). Besides trilaciclib treatment, only older age at baseline (for TP53 CH and DDR CH) and smaller VAF at baseline (for DDR CH) were predictive of higher CH growth rate during therapy (Supplementary Table 6). TP53-mutant MNs are driven by a combination of nonsense, frameshift and missense mutations. We observed a similar expansion of TP53-mutant clones during chemotherapy regardless of TP53 mutational type, with trilaciclib reducing the growth rate relative to the placebo arm (Extended Data Fig. 1g). This suggests that the reduced selection advantage of TP53-mutant CH during chemotherapy, observed with trilaciclib, occurs across a diverse spectrum of TP53 mutations.

sec.title: Trilaciclib reduces chemotherapy-induced TP53 CH expansion in mice
sec.p:
We then evaluated the functional effects of CDK4/6 inhibition on growth and characteristics of CH in response to cytotoxic chemotherapy in an experimental setting. We evaluated the impact of trilaciclib, alone or in combination with carboplatin, in mice, in which hematopoiesis comprised a small (~10%) proportion of Trp53-mutant cells. While we observed that trilaciclib reduced the fitness of multiple DDR CH mutations in humans, we chose to focus on TP53 as the clinical relevance of PPM1D and CHEK2 to MN development is less clear11,33–35. To accomplish this, 8-week-old CD45.1+ recipient C57/BL6 mice were lethally irradiated and engrafted with BM cells composed of a 9:1 ratio of CD45.1+ Vav-cre Trp53 wild-type (WT) cells and CD45.2+ Vav-cre Trp53R172H/WT cells or CD45.2+ Vav-cre Trp53WT cells (Fig. 3a). One month later, recipient mice were bled to analyze the chimerism of the peripheral blood. A total of ~10% peripheral blood was composed of CD45.2+ cells, reflecting a subclonal CH population comparable to the transplanted cell composition. Mice were then randomized to four treatment groups lasting for 4 weeks—vehicle control, carboplatin alone (30 mg kg−1 intraperitoneally twice per week), trilaciclib alone (100 mg kg−1 intraperitoneally twice per week) or carboplatin concomitant with trilaciclib (trilaciclib given 30 min before carboplatin administration).Fig. 3CDK4/6 inhibition mitigates the clonal advantage of Trp53-mutant CH in response to cytotoxic chemotherapy.
a, Schema of experiment to test the impact of carboplatin (‘carbo’), trilaciclib or the combination (combo) on hematopoiesis in mice containing an admixture of Trp53WT and Trp53R172H/WT hematopoietic cells. Lethally irradiated CD45.1+ recipient mice were engrafted with a 9:1 ratio of Vav-cre Trp53 WT cells from CD45.1+ donor mice (‘Vav-cre’) mixed with Trp53R172H/WT-mutant cells from CD45.2+ donor mice (‘Vav-cre Trp53R172H/WT’). An additional control cohort of CD45.1 recipient mice was engrafted with a 9:1 mix of Trp53WT CD45.1+ and CD45.2+ donor cells. One month later, mice were treated with vehicle, carboplatin (carbo), trilaciclib or the combination (combo) for 4 weeks at the indicated doses. Mice were bled pretreatment as well as weekly thereafter and killed at 4 weeks to evaluate chimerism in the BM. b, Ratio of CD45.2+/CD45.1+ cells among live, PBMNCs weekly before and during treatment. Data are represented as box-and-whisker plots where bar indicates median; box edges indicate the first and third quartile values; and whisker edges indicate minimum and maximum values (n = 10 mice per group). c, Representative FACS plots of data from b before therapy and at 4 weeks of treatment. d, Box-and-whisker plots of BM chimerism after 4 weeks of treatment (n = 10 mice per group). e, As in d but for percentage of LT-HSCs (Lin− c-Kit+ Sca-1+ CD150+ CD48−) in total LSK (Lin− c-Kit+ Sca-1+) cells (n = 10 mice per group). P values were determined using a one-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s test. Data are represented as box-and-whisker plots where the bar indicates median; box edges indicate the first and third quartile values; and whisker edges indicate minimum and maximum values. ANOVA, analysis of variance; FACS, fluorescence-activated cell sorting; PBMNCs, peripheral blood MNCs; i.p., intraperitoneally.

Peripheral blood was collected weekly to assess chimerism. Carboplatin resulted in a clonal advantage to Trp53R172H/WT-mutant cells, with the CD45.2+ cell population (reflecting Trp53R172H/WT-mutant cells) expanding from a mean of 18% (14–23%) to 45% (34–64%) after 4 weeks (Fig. 3b,c). There was no expansion of this population in mice treated with vehicle or trilaciclib alone. This result reflects the known fitness advantage of Trp53R172H/WT-mutant hematopoietic cells with cytotoxic chemotherapy10,12. In contrast, administration of trilaciclib and carboplatin completely abrogated the growth of Trp53R172H/WT-mutant cells. Evaluation of the CD45.2+ Vav-cre Trp53R172H/WT cell population composition in the peripheral blood revealed that, while carboplatin treatment increased monocytes and decreased B cells, concurrent administration of trilaciclib reversed these effects (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b).

After 4 weeks of treatment, animals were killed to evaluate chimerism of mature cells and HSPCs in the BM based on Trp53 genotype. Total BM MNC chimerism reflected peripheral blood findings; carboplatin alone resulted in increased frequency of Trp53R172H/WT-mutant cells, while concurrent administration of trilaciclib abrogated this effect (Fig. 3d). The combined treatment also significantly reduced Trp53-mutant long-term hematopoietic stem cells (LT-HSCs) and granulocyte/monocyte progenitor (GMP) cells (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 2c–e). Together, these results demonstrate that trilaciclib prevents chemotherapy-induced expansion of Trp53-mutant HSPCs, consistent with our observations in trilaciclib clinical trials.

CDK4/6 inhibitors as a class are known to cause dose-dependent cytopenias, including leukopenia and thrombocytopenia36. We therefore assessed the effects of each therapy on blood counts in mice with or without Trp53R172H/WT-mutant CH. Carboplatin treatment alone suppressed total white blood cell (WBC) counts, platelet counts and total BM MNC numbers in mice initially engrafted with 10% Trp53R172H/WT-mutant cells, which was not worsened by 4 weeks of combined carboplatin and trilaciclib (Extended Data Fig. 3a–c). Combined treatment resulted in a mild macrocytic anemia (Extended Data Fig. 3d,e). Overall, these data functionally support clinical trial findings that pharmacologic CDK4/6 inhibition is a sufficient and safe means to potentially prevent the clonal advantage of TP53-mutant hematopoietic cells during cytotoxic chemotherapy.

sec.title: Palbociclib reduces chemotherapy-induced TP53 CH expansion
sec.p: In contrast to trilaciclib, which is intravenously administered only before chemotherapy in patients with ES-SCLC, several oral CDK4/6 inhibitors are chronically administered daily for patients with hormone receptor-positive breast cancer. To evaluate whether the impact of CDK4/6 inhibitors on preventing chemotherapy-induced expansion of Trp53-mutant CH was consistent across classes of CDK4/6 inhibitors, we repeated the above in vivo experiments with the clinical oral CDK4/6 inhibitor palbociclib.

We tested the impact of 1 month of palbociclib (100 mg kg−1 daily for 5 days per week), carboplatin, the combination or vehicle treatment in CD45.1+ C57/B6 mice engrafted with a 9:1 ratio of CD45.1+ Vav-cre Trp53WT to CD45.2+ Vav-cre Trp53R172H/WT or CD45.2+ Vav-cre Trp53WT BM cells (Extended Data Fig. 4a). Again, carboplatin treatment expanded Trp53R172H/WT-mutant cells in the peripheral blood and BM (Extended Data Fig. 4b–d). Moreover, carboplatin increased the frequency of monocytes among CD45.2+ cells and the absolute number of Trp53R172H/WT-mutant LT-HSCs in the BM (Extended Data Fig. 4e and 5a). However, daily oral palbociclib therapy (administered 1 h before carboplatin treatment) abrogated the growth advantage of Trp53R172H/WT-mutant cells in the peripheral blood and BM and reduced the proportion of Trp53R172H/WT-mutant CD11b+Gr1+ myeloid cells.

Finally, we evaluated the proportion of Trp53-mutant and WT LT-HSCs undergoing apoptosis after 4 weeks of treatment. The analyses revealed an increase in BM annexin V+ LT-HSCs among Trp53-mutant cells in mice treated with both palbociclib and carboplatin relative to other treatment groups and relative to Trp53 WT LT-HSCs from the same animal (Extended Data Fig. 5b,c). Furthermore, palbociclib combined with carboplatin decreased annexin V+ Trp53WT LT-HSCs compared to carboplatin alone (Extended Data Fig. 5b,c). These data indicate a selective effect of CDK4/6 inhibition in promoting the death of Trp53-mutant cells in the setting of platinum chemotherapy and preservation of WT HSCs.

Given the marrow suppressive effects of chronic CDK4/6 inhibitor administration37,38, we also assessed the impact of combined weekly carboplatin and daily palbociclib on total WBC count, hematocrit and platelets. This revealed no worsened impact of palbociclib with carboplatin than the impact of either drug alone on total WBC, hemoglobin or platelets (Extended Data Fig. 6a–d).

sec.title: CDK6 inactivation reduces chemotherapy-induced TP53 CH expansion
sec.p: In addition to pharmacologically inhibiting CDK4/6, we also tested the effect of genetically manipulating CDK6 in response to platinum chemotherapy. We introduced a dominant negative form of Cdk6 (Cdk6 D163N39,40) into mouse BM cells with WT or mutant Trp53 (along with WT Cdk6 or an empty vector). We focused on genetic manipulation of CDK6, given extensive literature indicating that CDK6, but not CDK4, is required in hematopoietic cells38,41. Cells expressing WT and mutant Cdk6 (marked by GFP) were then mixed in a 1:9 ratio with Trp53 WT cells expressing RFP and the cell mixture was exposed in vitro to increasing doses of carboplatin for 72 h (Extended Data Fig. 7a,b). Flow cytometry analysis for GFP and RFP revealed expansion of Trp53-mutant cells expressing WT Cdk6 with carboplatin, while Trp53-mutant cells expressing dominant negative Cdk6 did not increase in frequency with carboplatin (Extended Data Fig. 7c,d). Overall, these genetic data further support the notion that CDK6 inhibition mitigates the growth of TP53-mutant CH in response to cytotoxic therapy.

sec.title: CDK4/6 inhibition reduces TP53 CH growth after therapy completion
sec.p:
In our samples obtained from patients receiving trilaciclib in clinical trials, long-term follow-up samples were not available to assess the durability of changes in CH clones to trilaciclib therapy. We repeated the competitive transplant experiment engrafting a 9:1 ratio of CD45.1+ Trp53 WT to CD45.2+ Trp53-mutant or WT cells (Fig. 4a). However, here mice were treated with trilaciclib, carboplatin, the combination or control for 2 weeks, followed by treatment cessation for 6 weeks. Hematopoietic cell chimerism was assessed weekly during and after drug treatment. In this experiment, the clonal advantage of Trp53R172H/WT-mutant cells remained elevated for several weeks after carboplatin cessation (Fig. 4b). However, 2 weeks of trilaciclib administration before carboplatin treatment were sufficient to prevent clonal expansion of Trp53R172H/WT-mutant cells for the duration of the experiment, including the 6-week drug discontinuation. sec.title: CDK4/6 inhibition promotes lymphopoiesis
sec.p: Cytotoxic chemotherapy results in functional attrition of normal HSCs through proliferative exhaustion and induces myeloid-biased differentiation while reducing adaptive cellular immunity17. In contrast, the dependence of HSCs on CDK4/6 for cell-cycle progression limits the proportion of HSCs susceptible to cell-cycle-dependent cytotoxic chemotherapies. To comprehensively characterize gene expression, cell cycle and lineage states across mouse HSPC and immune cells after in vivo treatment with carboplatin, trilaciclib or the combination, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) on BM CD45.2+ hematopoietic cells from recipient CD45.1+ mice engrafted with Vav-cre Trp53R172H/WT-mutant CH or Vav-cre control mice after 28 days of treatment. Sequenced cells were classified into 14 distinct clusters and annotated as multipotent progenitor (MPP), megakaryocyte/erythroid progenitor (MEP), early erythroid (Ery), common lymphoid progenitor (CLP), GMP, immature neutrophil precursors (immNeu), mature neutrophil (mNeu), polymorphonuclear (PMN), monocyte progenitor (mono.P), dendritic (DC), NK.T, early B, mature B or plasma cells (Extended Data Fig. 8a).

We evaluated the impact of each therapy on gene expression signatures of cell-cycle state and hematopoietic differentiation. Consistent with our mouse functional studies, carboplatin treatment significantly altered the composition of progenitor and immune cell populations in both Trp53 WT and mutant hematopoiesis. Among Trp53R172H/WT-mutant CH cells, carboplatin treatment expanded myeloid lineage progenitors, particularly immNeu as well as dendritic cells (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 8b). Notably, this myeloid progenitor expansion was reduced by trilaciclib treatment, which was associated with enrichment of lymphoid precursors, including CLP and early B cells (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 8b).

To determine the transcriptional signature governing treatment-associated lineage specification in HSC and MPPs, we performed transcription factor (TF) enrichment analyses and determined TF transcripts altered in HSC and MPPs in Trp53R172H/WT CH in response to different treatments (Extended Data Fig. 8c). This analysis revealed that trilaciclib treatment differentially upregulated lymphoid-specific TF expression (for example, Bcl6 and Bach2) and downregulated the expression of TFs that induce myeloid-erythroid fate in HSC (for example, Ybx1 and Xbp1), while carboplatin treatment induced myeloid-specific TF expression (Extended Data Fig. 8c). Given this finding, we evaluated the mRNA expression levels of lymphocyte-differentiation-related TFs in CLPs from Trp53WT (CD45.1+) and Trp53R172H mutant (CD45.2+) cells from the same mice treated with vehicle, carboplatin, trilaciclib or the combination. Consistent with the flow cytometric data demonstrating myeloid cell differentiation with carboplatin treatment alone in Trp53-mutant cells (Extended Data Figs. 2b and 5a), carboplatin treatment was not associated with increased lymphoid TF expression in Trp53-mutant cells (Extended Data Fig. 9a,b). However, the treatment with trilaciclib and/or the combination of trilaciclib, as well as carboplatin, increased lymphoid differentiation factor expression. These data, along with the finding that concomitant administration of trilaciclib suppresses myeloid cell expansion of Trp53-mutant cells seen with carboplatin alone, suggest that pretreatment with CDK4/6 inhibitor may promote lymphopoiesis in the setting of cytotoxic chemotherapy.

sec.title: CDK4/6 inhibition promotes apoptosis and cell-cycle arrest
sec.p: Prior work in rodents and patients demonstrates that CDK4/6 inhibition induces transient G1 cell-cycle arrest in HSPCs17. Similarly, scRNA-seq analyses revealed that trilaciclib increased the proportion of hematopoietic cells in G0/G1 phase and decreased the proportion of cells in S phase (Fig. 4e,f). These effects occurred regardless of Trp53 genotype of cells. However, carboplatin treatment dramatically increased the percentage of Trp53-mutant HSPCs in S phase, an effect not seen in Trp53 WT counterpart cells (Fig. 4d,e). Concomitant trilaciclib and carboplatin treatment were sufficient to suppress the effects of carboplatin treatment on the cell cycle and increased the frequency of Trp53-mutant hematopoietic cells in the G0/G1 phase (Fig. 4d,e). Moreover, Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) of differentially expressed pathways in MPP/HSCs from Trp53 WT and mutant mice revealed positive enrichment of gene sets associated with apoptosis in Trp53-mutant mice treated with trilaciclib (Extended Data Fig. 9c–f). In contrast, Trp53 WT MPP/HSCs had negative enrichment of gene sets associated with apoptosis in response to trilaciclib therapy or combined trilaciclib and carboplatin (Extended Data Fig. 9c–f). These gene expression findings are consistent with the functional assessment of apoptosis in animals treated with carboplatin with or without CDK4/6 inhibition in Extended Data Fig. 5, where CDK4/6 inhibition promoted early apoptosis of Trp53-mutant LT-HSCs while protecting Trp53 WT LT-HSCs from the death induced by platinum chemotherapy.

Analysis of CDK family member transcripts revealed that Cdk4 and Cdk6 expressions were significantly higher in Trp53R172H/WT-mutant HSC/MPP cells compared with control (Extended Data Fig. 9g). Given this finding, we evaluated the impact of platinum chemotherapy with or without contemporaneous CDK4/6 inhibition on stemness. We assigned stemness scores to cells based on several established HSC gene expression signatures29 (Extended Data Fig. 9h). As expected, stemness scores were highest among HSC and MPP and decreased along committed mature myeloid and lymphoid trajectories. Notably, carboplatin treatment elevated the stemness score of Trp53R172H/WT CH, while reducing control cell stemness (Fig. 4f). In contrast, trilaciclib treatment significantly suppressed chemotherapy-induced stemness upregulation. Altogether, these data indicate that CDK4/6 inhibition promotes mouse HSC and myeloid progenitor quiescence while mitigating the myeloid cell expansion and increased stemness advantage of Trp53-mutant mouse HSPCs observed in the setting of cytotoxic chemotherapy.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: tMN has long been recognized as a fatal consequence of exposure to cytotoxic therapy. While rare, patient populations at high risk for tMN have been established. This includes individuals receiving highly leukemogenic therapies42,43 and with pre-existing TP53 CH26,44,45. Avoidance of therapy is currently the only preventive strategy to reduce tMN risk, but it can lead to worse cancer outcomes. Here we show in four placebo-controlled randomized clinical trials of trilaciclib given in conjunction with a variety of chemotherapeutic regimens and across diverse patient populations that trilaciclib mitigates chemotherapy-related DDR CH expansion, including TP53. This finding was also observed in a syngeneic mouse model of TP53 CH, demonstrating that CDK4/6 inhibition blocks platinum-induced mutant TP53 competitive repopulation through promoting HSPC quiescence and apoptosis. Moreover, our studies also confirmed prior data identifying that CDK4/6 inhibition protects mouse TP53 WT HSPCs from cell death induced by genotoxic therapies16,17,46. These cumulative effects ultimately manifested as a decreased TP53-mutant CH advantage in response to platinum chemotherapy across archival patient specimens and mouse in vivo studies. This represents a proof-of-concept demonstration of a potential pharmacologic strategy to block chemotherapy-induced expansion of preleukemic TP53-mutant clones.

TP53 is a commonly mutated gene in both therapy-related and de novo MN with a diverse spectrum of nonsense, frameshift and missense mutations. While our mouse model was restricted to the R172H hotspot mutation, given that we observed a similar protective effect of trilaciclib in preventing expansion of both loss-of-function and missense mutations within our clinical trial data, we anticipate that our findings may extend across pathogenic TP53 variants. Beyond exposure to cytotoxic therapy, the risk factors for mutant TP53-driven MNs are unclear. However, other forms of cellular stress, such as defective ribosomal assembly in Schwachman–Diamond syndrome, have been shown to promote TP53-related CH and malignant transformation47,48. The potential for CDK4/6 inhibition to mitigate the competitive advantage of TP53-mutant cells under other forms of genotoxic stress was not established in this study, but it is a critical question for future inquiry. While our mouse data support that the protective effect of CDK4/6 inhibition persists after therapy cessation, longer-term follow-up in human studies is needed to clarify the extent of durability and the optimal duration of CDK4/6 inhibitor treatment.

Clonal expansion of CH, including TP53 CH, is a well-established risk factor for MN development and indeed a critical component of the natural history of CH progression to MN10,12. None of the patients in our study developed a hematologic malignancy that is not unexpected given the sample size and the short median duration of follow-up (<2 years for all trials; Supplementary Tables 7–9). The vast majority of TP53 clones observed had a low VAF (<2%) even after the treatment. These small clones, although unlikely to cause immediate tMN, represent the earliest stage of tMN development. Ultimately, prospective trials are needed to fully evaluate the potential for CDK4/6 inhibitor to prevent tMN. Patients with cancers that are independent of CDK4/6 and at high risk for tMN would be ideal candidates for such studies, as existing clinical data suggest that CDK4/6 inhibitors do not interfere with the antitumor efficacy of chemotherapy in these cases. While the vast majority (70%) of solid tumors are neither highly dependent nor independent on CDK4/6 (ref. 49), preclinical evidence suggests that CDK4/6 inhibition may not only be compatible with chemotherapy in tumors with intermediate CDK4/6 dependence50 but may also enhance antitumor efficacy by preserving immune function51,52. However, this may vary by regimen and tumor characteristics. Indeed, in the CRC randomized trial, while trilaciclib reduced myelosuppression, early antitumor endpoints favored placebo (Supplementary Table 9)30. There are 24 ongoing clinical trials of trilaciclib combined with additional chemotherapeutic regimens. Evaluation of these ongoing studies will clarify the safety of trilaciclib when combined with additional cytotoxic therapies across various patient populations and inform the development of tMN chemoprevention trials for CDK4/6 inhibitors.

While diverse mechanisms drive the competitive advantage of specific CH mutations, a common pathway is the regulation of HSPC stemness53 that is highly dependent on CDK4/6 (refs. 54,55). Here we focused on trilaciclib, a transient CDK4/6 inhibitor, given in conjunction with chemotherapy. Whether chronic CDK4/6 inhibition, in the absence of chemotherapy, might decrease the fitness advantage of CH more broadly, beyond DDR-mutant clones, was not evaluated here and represents an attractive avenue for future investigation.

sec.title: Clinical samples
sec.p: We obtained serial blood samples from four randomized clinical trials of intravenous trilaciclib (240 mg m−2) conducted by G1 Therapeutics. Eligible patients for all four studies were aged at least 18 years, with Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status 0‒2, and adequate organ function. The original clinical studies were designed and conducted in compliance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and the Good Clinical Practice guidelines of the International Council for Harmonisation. The study protocol and all study-related materials were approved by the institutional review board (IRB) or independent ethics committee of each investigational site. The first two trials evaluated trilaciclib versus placebo administered in conjunction with carboplatin and etoposide with or without atezolizumab in individuals with ES-SCLC—G1T28-05 (NCT03041311; CGIRB ICO2-15-259) and G1T28-02 (NCT02499770; Advarra, Pro00026391)25. Trilaciclib or placebo was administered before carboplatin and etoposide with or without atezolizumab on days 1–3 of each 21-day cycle for up to 4 cycles. Blood samples were available from cycle 1 day 1 (C1D1) immediately before treatment and after four 21-day cycles. For the purposes of our analyses regarding the impact of trilaciclib on CH, we combined data from the two SCLC trials (Supplementary Table 7). The third trial evaluated trilaciclib with leucovorin/5-fluorouracil/oxaliplatin/irinotecan, as well as bevacizumab, among individuals with mCRC (NCT04607668; WIRB 20202554)30. Patients received trilaciclib or placebo immediately before chemotherapy on days 1 and 2 of each 14-day cycle. Blood samples were available from C1D1 and after 12 14-day cycles (Supplementary Table 8). The fourth trial evaluated trilaciclib with gemcitabine and carboplatin among women with mTNBC (NCT02978716; WIRB 20162457)31. Patients were randomized to receive trilaciclib or placebo on days 1 and 8 immediately before chemotherapy. Blood samples were available from C1D1 and after seven 21-day cycles (Supplementary Table 9). Patient demographics were comparable between the trilaciclib and the placebo groups in all four studies. As a comparison cohort, serial samples from age-matched healthy individuals who were not being treated for cancer (n = 176) were obtained from the Knight Center Alzheimer’s Disease Research Cohorts56, which was approved by the IRB of Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis (IRB 201109148). Finally, as a set of technical controls (that is, panel of normals (PoN)), blood samples were obtained from 7 children (<15 years old) and 20 young adults (<40 years old), which was approved by the IRB of BJC WEBB (IRB 202012143). Written informed consent was obtained from each patient or participant before initiation of all study procedures.

sec.title: Sequencing
sec.p: Blood samples were sequenced using a custom-designed DNA sequencing assay (VariantPlex, ArcherDX, Integrated DNA Technologies). The custom panel included nine of the most commonly mutated genes found in solid tumor patients with CH12 and captured the full exonic regions of five genes (DNMT3A, TET2, ASXL1, TP53, CHEK2), as well as the partial exonic regions of four genes (JAK2, SRSF2, SF3B1, PPM1D). Libraries were prepared from 250-ng genomic DNA derived from peripheral blood MNCs using the VariantPlex protocol that uses anchored multiplex PCR to generate target-enriched libraries. After enzymatic DNA fragmentation, each DNA strand was ligated with a molecular barcode, thereby tagging it with a unique molecular index (UMI) enabling error-corrected sequencing. Libraries were sequenced on a NovaSeq 6000 or NovaSeqX (Illumina) to yield a mean coverage of 27,665× per base after consensus sequence building. We removed samples with a mean coverage under 1,000×.

sec.title: Variant calling
sec.p: After demultiplexing, raw FASTQ files were processed through the ArCH variant-calling pipeline26. The ArCH variant-calling pipeline is an end-to-end CH variant-calling workflow, designed to be used on deep UMI-based sequencing approaches that have been previously experimentally validated to reliably detect variants down to 0.1% VAF with 92.6% sensitivity and 91% positive predictive value. ArCH leverages an ensemble variant-calling approach using three separate variant callers (Mutect2 (ref. 57), VarDict58 and LoFreq2 (ref. 59)) and postvariant calling filters to remove putative artifacts and germline variants. In cases where mutations were identified at only one time point, we used mpileup (BCFtools60) to query the sequencing data for evidence of the mutation at the other time point. A Fisher’s exact test was conducted to statistically compare the signal detected by the pileup against the PoN samples. If the VAF was higher in the sample compared to the PoN, the variant was retained. Overall, we restricted our analysis to include mutations above 0.1% VAF in at least one time point. In addition, for variants under 0.2% VAF, to ensure high precision, we required a minimum of 17,000 total read depth (Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4). ArCH features a functional annotation pipeline using prior published data and curated clinical databases to identify putative driver CH variants (in-depth details can be found within the Supplementary Methods).

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: For each mutation detected in both pretreatment and post-treatment samples, the growth rate was calculated as ln(V/V0)/(T − T0)12, with T and T0 indicating the age of the individual (in days) at each serially obtained time point, and V and V0 corresponding to the VAF of the mutation at T and T0, respectively (Supplementary Table 3). Logistic regression was used to compare the odds of harboring a CH mutation between the placebo and trilaciclib groups. Linear regression was used to compare the differences in growth rates of CH mutations between treatment cohorts. We performed regressions comparing models adjusted for only age and adjusted for age as well as sex, race, clinical trial cohort and change in blood counts, with similar results. Because full demographic data were only available on a subset of patients, in our main results, we show the results from models adjusted for age only unless otherwise indicated. Statistical analyses were performed using R (v4.3.2).

sec.title: Mixed BM chimera mouse transplants
sec.p: Mice were housed and maintained in a pathogen-free facility. Up to five mice were housed together in each cage and maintained on a 12-h light/12-h dark cycle, with access to autoclaved food and water.

Point mutant Trp53 (B6.129S4(Cg)-Trp53tm2.1Tyj/J, hereafter called Trp53 R172H (B6)) founder mice were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory (Bar Harbor). These mice were cross-bred with Vav-cre mice to generate Vav-cre Trp53R172H/WT litters and Vav-cre Trp53WT. Three weeks after birth, animals were weaned, and tails were collected for genotyping. All procedures performed in the study followed the National Institute of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and were approved by the Committee on Ethics of Animal Experiments of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center.

For competitive transplantation, 0.1 × 106 BM (CD45.2+) from either Vav-cre Trp53WT or Vav-cre Trp53R172H/WT litters were mixed with 0.9 × 106 BM (CD45.1+) at a 1:9 ratio and injected through tail vein into lethally irradiated Pep/BoyJ CD45.1+ mice (900 rad). After 2 weeks, engraftment was confirmed by flow cytometry with anti-CD45.2 and anti-CD45.1. In subsequent weeks, peripheral blood was obtained from maxillary bleeds and collected in ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid tubes for monthly flow cytometry and complete blood count analyses using a Sysmex SN series analyzer (Sysmex), followed by differential counting. Mice were killed when they showed any signs of disease (for example, weight loss, hind limb paralysis, lethargy, hunched posture or difficulty in breathing) and tissues were collected to be further processed for pathological analysis. In selected experiments, single-cell suspensions of blood, spleen and BM were analyzed by flow cytometry for lineage markers as well as Sca-1 and c-Kit upon live cell gating using BD Fortessa. The frequency of stem/progenitor cells were analyzed based on staining of markers (CD48, CD150, CD34 and CD16/CD32).

sec.title: Competitive assay of mouse BM cells overexpressing Cdk6 constructs
sec.p: Mouse Cdk6 WT (Cdk6-WT) and kinase-dead dominant-negative (Cdk6 D163N) cDNA constructs were obtained from Addgene (plasmids 75173 and 75170 (ref. 61)) and subcloned into the retroviral pMIG-II vector containing enhanced GFP (EGFP). Retroviral particles were generated by cotransfection of 293FT cells with pMIG-II-RFP, pMIG-II-EGFP, Cdk6 WT-pMIG-II-EGFP or Cdk6 D163N-pMIG-II-EGFP, along with the packaging plasmid pCL-Eco, using polyethylenimine transfection reagent. Plasmid sequences and open reading frames were validated by whole plasmid nanopore sequencing. Viral supernatants were concentrated using Retro-X concentrator (Takara) and used to infect primary mouse BM cells. CD45.2⁺ BM cells were isolated from Vav-cre Trp53WT/WT or Trp53R172H/WT mice, and CD45.1⁺ competitor cells were isolated from congenic CD45.1⁺ Pep/BoyJ mice. CD45.2⁺ cells were transduced with EGFP-tagged retrovirus (expressing control, Cdk6 WT or Cdk6 D163N), and CD45.1⁺ cells were transduced with RFP expressing control retrovirus by spinfection at 2,600 rpm for 100 min on retronectin-coated plates. Viral titers were optimized to achieve transduction efficiencies >95%. After infection, CD45.2⁺ and CD45.1⁺ cells were mixed at a 1:9 ratio and cultured in mouse HSC expansion medium62,63. Cultures were treated with increasing concentrations (0, 100 and 200 nM) of carboplatin for 72 h. The ratio of GFP+ to RFP+ viable cells was quantified by flow cytometry (BD Fortessa) to assess relative fitness under genotoxic stress.

sec.title: Flow cytometry in mouse peripheral blood and BM
sec.p: Lineages of primary and engrafted cells were identified with the following markers: APC-Cy7-CD45.1 (A20), PE-CD45.2 (104), FITC-CD11b (M1/70), APC-Gr-1 (R86-8C5), PerCP5.5-B220 (RA3-6B2) and BV711-CD3 (17A2). Stem/progenitor cells were identified with the following markers: Pacific Blue Lineage (a cocktail of CD3e, Ly6G/Ly6C, CD11b, CD45R/B220, TER119), FITC-CD34 (RAM34), BUV395-CD117 (2B8), AF700-Sca-1 (D7), BV711-CD48 (hm48-1), APC-CD150 (Q38-480), PE-CD16/32 (2.4G2), APC-Cy7-CD45.1 (A20) and BV605-CD45.2 (104). The immunophenotypic cell surface antigens are as follows: LT-HSC (Lin− c-Kit+ Sca-1+ CD48− CD150+), ST-HSC (Lin− c-Kit+ Sca-1+ CD48− CD150−), MPPs (Lin− c-Kit+ Sca-1+ CD48+ CD150−), LSK (Lin− c-Kit+ Sca-1+), GMP (Lin− c-Kit+ Sca-1− CD16/32+ CD34+), common myeloid progenitors (Lin− c-Kit+ Sca-1− CD16/32− CD34+) and MEPs (Lin− c-Kit+ Sca-1− CD16/32− CD34−). Subsequently, the stained cells were analyzed by BD Fortessa. Antibodies were purchased from BioLegend or BD (Supplementary Table 10).

For annexin V and 7-AAD staining, BM cells stained with the above HSC/progenitor flow panels were washed and resuspended with annexin V binding buffer (422201, BioLegend) and subsequently stained with FITC–anti-annexin V (1:1,000; 640922, BioLegend) and 7-AAD (420403, BioLegend) in annexin V binding buffer for 15 min at room temperature. The cells were resuspended with 300-µl annexin V binding buffer and analyzed using flow cytometry.

sec.title: Trilaciclib
sec.p: Half of the engrafted 6-week-old to 8-week-old female B6.SJL-Ptprca Pepcb/BoyJ mice were treated with intraperitoneal injection of trilaciclib (100 mg kg−1), and the other half with vehicle (50 mM citrate buffer) solution (twice per week). Thirty minutes later, a single intraperitoneal injection of carboplatin (30 mg kg−1) or 0.9% NaCl vehicle control was given to these mice twice per week. Treated mice were monitored daily for body condition and/or weight loss, and killed if they developed severe deterioration of body condition, paralysis and/or loss of more than 20% body weight.

sec.title: Palbociclib
sec.p: Half of the engrafted 6-week-old to 8-week-old female B6.SJL-Ptprca Pepcb/BoyJ mice were given oral gavage of palbociclib (100 mg kg−1; S1116, Selleckchem), and the other half vehicle (0.9% NaCl; daily). A single intraperitoneal injection of carboplatin (30 mg kg−1) or 0.9% NaCl vehicle control was given to these mice twice per week, 1 h after palbociclib administration. Treated mice were monitored daily for body condition and/or weight loss, and killed if they developed severe deterioration of body condition, paralysis and/or loss of more than 20% body weight.

sec.title: Cellular indexing of transcriptomes and library construction
sec.p: BM cells from Vav-cre Trp53WT or Vav-cre Trp53R172H/WT mice receiving treatments (three mice per treatment/genotype group) were washed twice with cold PBS before labeling with unique TotalSeqA-compatible HashTags (BioLegend). Subsequently, samples were incubated with mouse Fc receptor-blocking agent (BioLegend) and labeled with DAPI for live cell sorting by flow cytometry using an Aria cytometer (BD Biosciences). After sorting, equal numbers of cells were pooled and submitted to the MSKCC Integrative Genomics Core for sequencing. A 10x Genomics Chromium machine was used for 3,000–5,000 single-cell capture. Cells were washed and partitioned into nanoliter-scale Gel Bead-In-Emulsions (GEMs), where all generated cDNA share a common 10x Genomics Barcode but use a pool of ~750,000 barcodes to index each cell’s transcriptome. The silane magnetic beads and Solid Phase Reversible Immobilization beads were used to clean up the GEM reaction mixture and the barcoded cDNA was then amplified in a PCR step. Libraries were prepared using the Chromium Single Cell 3′ Reagent Kits (v3.1)—Single Cell 3′ Library & Gel Bead Kit (v3.1), Single Cell 3′ Chip G Kit (v3.1) and Single Index kit T Set A (10x Genomics). Libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq using paired-end 75-bp reads. The P7 and R2 primers were added during the GEM incubation and the P5 and R1 during library construction through end repair, A-tailing, adaptor ligation and PCR. The final libraries contain the P5 and P7 primers used in Illumina bridge amplification.

sec.title: scRNA-seq data analysis
sec.p: FASTQ reads were processed using the Cell Ranger (v7.0.0) ‘count’ workflow to generate gene expression and antibody capture data matrices. In addition, the Cell Ranger ‘multi’ pipeline was executed to demultiplex hashed sequencing samples. The resulting filtered sparse count matrices were loaded into R (v4.0.0) as Seurat (v4.0.6) objects. Multiplets were identified using scDblFinder (v1.10.0) and removed. Further filtering retained (1) RNA features detected in more than three cells and (2) cells with more than 200 and fewer than 2,500 detected features. miQC (v1.10.0) was used to identify and filter out low-quality cells based on mitochondrial gene detection and UMI distributions, using a posterior cutoff of 0.95 and flexmix spline models. As a result, 6,258 cells were removed, and 134,353 cells were retained. Seurat (v4.4.0) was used for data normalization and scaling, focusing on 4,000 highly variable genes. Twenty-five principal components were used for unsupervised clustering and dimensionality reduction. The open-tSNE was generated based on a previously published pipeline64. Different cell-cycle stages were identified using Tricycle (v1.10.0). The cell-cycle stages were defined as follows: 0.5π as the start of the S stage, π as the start of the G2M stage, 1.5π as the middle of the M stage and 1.75–0.25π as the G1/G0 stage65. The relative proportions of cell populations and different cell-cycle stages were visualized using ggalluvial (v0.12.5). Stemness scores were quantified using mouse HSPC gene signatures66. Differentially expressed genes between trilaciclib-treated and nontreated samples were identified using the Wilcoxon test in FindAllMarkers, with a cutoff of P < 0.05 and |avg_log2(fold change (FC)) | > 0.1. A heatmap was used to visualize the significant genes of HSC/MPP across different groups.

The Reactome Cell Cycle pathway from the Molecular Signatures Database (v7.1) was used to compute correlation-based gene module scores for myeloid-biased MPP cells67. Scaled gene expression values (scale.data) were extracted for genes in the CELL_CYCLE gene set, and the average expression of these genes was computed under a specific condition. The Pearson correlation coefficient was then calculated between this average expression profile and the expression values of each individual MPP cell across the full gene set. Similarly, the ‘REACTOME:G0 AND EARLY G1’ and GO ‘G0 TO G1 TRANSITION’ gene sets were integrated to calculate G0/G1 scores following the same procedure.

To assess the balance between G0/G1 scores and proliferative activity in MPP cells, both the proliferation and G0/G1 scores were extracted and normalized to a (0,1) scale using min–max normalization. To decouple overlapping contributions, the normalized proliferation score was subtracted from the G0/G1 score, followed by renormalization of the residual G0/G1 values. For visualization across conditions, both scores were standardized (z normalized) and clipped to the range of ±0.3. Each MPP cell was then classified into one of four quadrants based on the signs of its normalized scores. Quadrant distributions were quantified across experimental conditions to determine the proportion of cells occupying each quadrant, using functions from the dplyr package. Density contour plots for each condition were generated using geom_density_2d() from ggplot2, with cells plotted in a two-dimensional space defined by the G0/G1 score (x axis) and the proliferation score (y axis).

The resulting scores were added as a new metadata column in the Seurat object. Violin plots were generated using the ggviolin() function from the ggpubr (v0.6.0) package, displaying lymphoid activation and differentiation scores across treatment groups (vehicle, carboplatin, trilaciclib and combination). Statistical significance was assessed using two-sided Student’s t tests among treatment pairs, with median trends highlighted.

sec.title: GSEA
sec.p: GSEA was conducted using the GSEA function from the clusterProfiler package (v3.14.3) to evaluate pathway-level enrichment across HALLMARK, GO and REACTOME gene sets. For each comparison, trilaciclib versus vehicle and combination therapy versus carboplatin in Trp53(R172H), as well as Vav-cre mice-derived MPP/HSC, a ranked gene list was generated based on the log2 FC values obtained from differential expression analysis. Differential expression was performed using the DESeq2 package (v1.26.0), and genes were ranked in descending order of log(FC) to prioritize upregulated genes.

GSEA was performed using the default parameters of clusterProfiler::GSEA, which estimates enrichment scores (ESs) by a permutation-based approach (nPerm = 1,000 by default). P values were calculated by comparing the observed ES against the distribution of ESs generated from random permutations of the gene labels. These nominal P values were quantified and finally labeled in Extended Data Fig. 9e. To visualize the enrichment results, the gseaplot2 function from the enrichplot package (v1.22.0) was used, focusing in particular on the HALLMARK:APOPTOSIS pathway. Ridge plots summarizing positively enriched pathways were generated to display the normalized ESs across different treatment comparisons.
